analysis.title: A Data Centre Boom Built for Yesterday's AI
key_insights: Nordea argues the assumptions behind the data centre buildout are starting to crack, chiefly that demand for computing power will keep growing exponentially.
A Columbia Business School report (Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh) says US data centre owners need total data centre revenue of 9-14% of projected US GDP by 2032 to earn a 10% return.
Growth in AI model size has slowed, but the most widely used AI services still run on large models, which has kept demand for data centre capacity high.

A Stanford study cited by the Financial Times finds smaller models can match, and in some cases outperform, larger models on the simpler queries that dominate current chat usage, and are improving quickly on reasoning tasks.
The IEA says a small language model can use as little as 3% of the energy of a large reasoning model. Nordea expects a growing share of inference demand to migrate to smaller, cheaper models.
AI demand is cost-sensitive. A KPMG survey found 49% of business leaders had scaled back, postponed or paused AI initiatives because expected costs were too high.

The Silicon Data LLM Token Expenditure Index, the usage-weighted price paid per million tokens, has fallen to around half its May peak. Most of the decline is attributed to traffic moving to cheaper Chinese open-weight models, also visible on OpenRouter.
Smaller models that run on laptops, phones and other devices could bypass data centres. Local AI is cheaper after the hardware purchase and keeps sensitive data on the device.
Nvidia has moved into computers designed to run AI locally with partners such as Dell and Lenovo. Nordea reads this as a sign of demand for local AI and of where Nvidia expects the market to go.

Other risks to the buildout: power generation and grid capacity may not expand fast enough, capital inflows raise overcrowding risk, and much of the expansion is debt-financed, which exposes it to higher rates and weaker revenues.

The buildout depends on AI labs surviving and scaling to pay for their compute commitments. The WSJ estimates OpenAI plans about $750bn of compute spend through 2030, and Anthropic's S-1 suggests commitments above $600bn over a longer period.

A large AI data centre takes three to five years from planning to operation, so capacity planned today may not run fully until the end of the decade. Nordea calls this a structural mismatch between certain commitments and an uncertain future.

sector_views.rationale: Nordea questions whether demand assumptions hold as smaller models and local AI take share, and cites power constraints, debt financing and the long build timeline as further risks.

risk_factors: Demand for computing power may not keep growing exponentially as smaller models gain capability.
Cost-sensitive AI buyers are shifting to cheaper models and scaling back AI projects.
Local AI on laptops and phones could bypass data centres.
Power generation and grid capacity may not keep pace with the buildout.
Overcrowding as many companies build on similar demand expectations.
Debt-financed expansion is vulnerable to higher interest rates and weaker revenues.
AI labs must survive and scale to pay their compute commitments.
The 3-5 year build time creates a mismatch with fast-changing AI demand.

tension_points.bull_case: Large models still power the most widely used AI services, and frontier models will keep playing an important role, which has kept data centre demand high.
tension_points.bear_case: Smaller models match larger ones on common queries at a fraction of the energy and cost, cost-sensitive buyers are shifting to them, and local AI could bypass data centres.

theme_stances.key_argument: Smaller, cheaper models and local AI may take a growing share of demand while the capacity planned today takes years to come online.
theme_stances.evidence: we are making fairly certain commitments for a fairly uncertain future

theme_stances.key_argument: Good-enough smaller models are cheaper to run, so a growing share of inference demand migrates toward them.
